title: Sobraon, 1846
hookLine: the Sikh army is defeated on the Sutlej, and Sikh memory holds that some of its own commanders betrayed it

cards: An old general gets dressed for battle in white. Sikh tradition remembers him that way: Sham Singh Attariwala, gray-bearded, in white clothes, mounting his horse on the morning of the fight.

In that telling, the white means he didn't expect to come home. Behind him the Sikh army is dug in along the bank of the Sutlej, with a bridge of boats at its back. In front of it, the British are forming up.

teach.b: At Sobraon the Khalsa army held strong earthworks on the river, and the British attacked them head on. The fighting was fierce, and for a time the Sikh lines held.
Then the British broke through, and the Sikh soldiers were pushed back toward the river.

teach.h: THE BRIDGE OF BOATS GIVES WAY.
teach.b: Behind them stood the bridge of boats, their road home.
Accounts say that Tej Singh, the commander, crossed back over it early, and that the bridge then broke, whether by the river, by the weight of men, or, as some tell it, by someone's order.
With the bridge gone, soldiers were trapped against the water. Many died in the Sutlej that day, histories say, and few surrendered. The old general in white rode into the fighting and fell there.
Sikh memory holds Sham Singh up beside the trapped soldiers as the honor of that day: men who were let down, and fought on anyway.
Sikh memory also holds that the army's own commanders, Tej Singh and the minister Lal Singh, betrayed it, sending word to the British and leading their own soldiers badly on purpose.
Cunningham, the British officer who wrote a history of the Sikhs, said much the same. Some historians weigh the evidence differently.
But the hurt in the story isn't hard to understand. An enemy across the river is expected. A commander behind you who wants you to lose is something else.

how: Sikhs remember Sobraon with grief and honor, telling of Sham Singh Attariwala and the soldiers trapped at the river, and of commanders Sikh memory holds to have betrayed them.

games.why: Sikh tradition remembers him in white, riding into the fighting at Sobraon, where he fell.

practice: If it feels safe, bring to mind a time someone you trusted let you down, not the worst one, a middle-sized one, and notice where it still sits in your body: chest, jaw, stomach.
Breathe into that place; you don't have to forgive or decide anything right now, only let the breath go there and be held. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Sobraon. The battle on the Sutlej where the Khalsa army was defeated, the bridge of boats gave way, and Sham Singh Attariwala fell.
